articles.title: CJP says Mumbai Police denied permission for Oct 2 protest, launches  ‘Jail Bharo Andolan’
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Sunday claimed that Mumbai Police had denied permission for its proposed protest on October 2.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Sunday claimed that Mumbai Police had denied permission for its proposed protest on October 2. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke announced that the outfit would launch a "jail bharo andolan" in Mumbai on Gandhi Jayanti if it was not allowed to demonstrate.Dipke said the police decision was another attempt to prevent citizens from raising their voices. He announced the proposed agitation in a post on X."Such tactics to suppress citizens’ voices are unacceptable. If we are denied the right to protest, CJP will launch a Jail Bharo Andolan in Mumbai on Gandhi Jayanti," Dipke said.The proposed protest comes amid a broader confrontation between the CJP and authorities after the outfit recently alleged that its co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka and volunteers were detained by police in Assam.Earlier detention in AssamThe CJP had on Sunday claimed that Ranka and around 40 volunteers were detained in Guwahati without being told the reason for the action.Ranka had travelled to Assam to meet CJP volunteers at the residence of opposition Assam Jatiya Parishad leader Kunki Chowdhury in the Dispur area, near the state secretariat. Dipke alleged that the group was prevented from holding the meeting."The Assam Police has detained Ashutosh Ranka and a CJP team, and is taking them to an unknown location. Ashu and co were going to have a small volunteers meet up in Assam," Dipke had said in a social media post.In another post, he said Ranka had been picked up from a private residence and claimed that neither he nor the other volunteers had been told the charges or grounds for the detention."If Ashu is not released, I will go to Assam along with other CJP members. (CM) Himanta (Biswa Sarma) can arrest us all," Dipke had said.A video posted on Ranka's X account showed him sitting in a moving police vehicle. He was heard alleging that Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma had ordered the action because he was "afraid" of the CJP's plans to highlight the condition of schools in the state.Talking to reporters while being taken away, Ranka alleged that the action showed the chief minister was "afraid of being exposed"."He (Sarma) is scared that if we show the schools here, the country will know the reality. He is afraid that people will know how their rights were being snatched in Kaziranga for the benefit of corporates. Also, man-made floods have taken scores of lives.“But, we are not afraid of him. We know that he won the assembly election by redrawing boundaries of constituencies," Ranka alleged.NCP (SP) backs CJP allegationsNCP (SP) spokesperson Anish Gawande later claimed that Ranka and 41 others had been "illegally and unconstitutionally detained from a private residence when a meet up was scheduled to take place with CJP volunteers".Gawande alleged that no legal notice had been served on the group and that they had not been informed of the sections imposed against them."It is nothing short of jungle raj under CM Sarma, who is afraid of any and all kind of dissent," Gawande said.He said the CJP had planned to raise issues including the condition of schools, evictions in Kaziranga, the arrest of activists and the alleged redrawing of election boundaries.“This is a pattern in Assam, happening here for too long. Pranab Doley gets picked up when he gets bail, and the NSA is invoked against him,” Gawande said, referring to the activist who had led protests in Kaziranga over the rights of indigenous people."This is another attempt to intimidate civil society and activists in Assam to create a police state," he asserted.“We demand the immediate release of Ranka and all others, failing which legal action will be taken against the Assam Police and no one less than the chief minister, himself, who has authorised this illegal action,” Gawande added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Switzerland rejects stricter interpretation of its neutrality
articles.summary: The initiative would have prevented the nation from imposing sanctions unless approved by the UN.
articles.body:
Voters in Switzerland have overwhelmingly rejected a stricter interpretation of the country's tradition of diplomatic neutrality.

More than 70% of Swiss voters rejected proposals that would have prevented the European nation from imposing sanctions without UN approval, official results showed.

The move would have also prevented Switzerland from pursuing closer ties with the Nato military alliance.

Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has reopened the debate around Switzerland's centuries-old non-alignment.

Moscow openly backed the initiative, which was supported by the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) and opposed by the federal government and all other major parties.

Lukas Golder, co-director of research institute Gfs.bern told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that Swiss voters had not rejected embracing its neutrality but that the vote showed Switzerland was in favour of sanctions against Russia.

"People have a clear idea of what Switzerland's neutrality is supposed to achieve," he said.

Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said during a recent televised debate that "neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility".

While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, including Ukraine, he stressed that "neutrality does not mean indifference".

He added that Switzerland would "not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace".

Switzerland was internationally recognised in 1815 when the country was granted "eternal neutrality" at the Congress of Vienna, during a period of war and upheaval in Europe.

This neutrality was legally defined by the Hague Convention of 1907, which forbade Switzerland supplying weapons to countries at war. It previously rejected a request from Germany for ammunition for tanks being sent to Kyiv.

Switzerland remained neutral through World War Two. It also banked gold looted by the Nazis and, in a move designed to keep Nazi Germany from invading, turned away thousands of Jewish refugees.

Switzerland apologised for the policies in the 1990s.

Switzerland's system of direct democracy means major political decisions are often deferred to the voters through referenda.

articles.title: Powerful nor’easter floods Northeast, leaves over 130,000 without power as high tides threaten coast
articles.summary: A powerful nor’easter battered the Northeast again on Sunday, flooding coastal communities and leaving tens of thousands of homes and businesses without power as forecasters warned that another round of high tides could inundate vulnerable shorelines.
articles.body: BOSTON — A powerful nor’easter battered the Northeast again on Sunday, flooding coastal communities and leaving tens of thousands of homes and businesses without power as forecasters warned that another round of high tides could inundate vulnerable shorelines. The slow-moving storm, which killed a New York City housing authority worker when a tree fell Saturday, was expected to linger through Sunday with heavy rain, strong winds and dangerous surf from New Jersey to New England. The storm remained just south of Long Island and east of northern New Jersey on Sunday morning and was expected to loop around the area for roughly another 24 hours, said Bob Oravec, a lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland. The worst of the remaining rainfall was expected Sunday from northern New Jersey through New York City and Long Island into southern New England. The storm was gradually weakening, Oravec said, but the threat of tidal flooding would linger through high-tide cycles Sunday morning and again in the evening. “The most impactful parts of the storm are likely going to be the high winds and the tidal flooding,” Oravec said. The nor’easter triggered memories of Superstorm Sandy, which left behind over $60 billion in damage across the eastern U.S. in 2012. While this storm’s impact has been nowhere near that, it could be the first of several along the East Coast this fall because of an El Niño climate pattern that’s disrupting this year’s weather. More than 130,000 customers were without power across the Northeast and mid-Atlantic Sunday morning, according to PowerOutage.us. The most widespread outages were along the New Jersey shore, New York’s Long Island and coastal counties in Connecticut. Toppled trees across Long Island damaged homes and cars, blocked streets and downed numerous utility lines. The Federal Emergency Management Agency said response coordination centers in impacted regions were operating at an “enhanced posture,” and teams were on standby in New England in case of widespread outages. On Saturday in New Jersey and New York, some people kayaked down flooded streets. Others headed to beaches to try to surf the higher-than-usual waves. Emergency crews in Sea Bright, New Jersey, rescued a woman and her dog after their vehicle became trapped in floodwaters, ABC7 reported. In Surf City, New Jersey, water rose inside a marina where workers had moved equipment to higher ground, and owner Kenny Formica said customers reported boats and Jet Skis missing or blown from their lifts. In Norfolk, Virginia, floodwaters left passing cars pushing wakes through some streets. The storm also disrupted travel throughout the region. Hundreds of flights were canceled at Boston Logan International Airport, while flooding cut off highway access to North Carolina’s Hatteras Island, stranding visitors and forcing one couple to scramble to relocate their wedding after most of their roughly 45 guests were unable to reach the island.

articles.title: What we know about RAF Fairford incident and counter-terror probe
articles.summary: Five men have been arrested as counter-terror police lead an investigation into a major incident near the airbase.
articles.body:
Five men have been arrested on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offences after a major incident was declared at an airbase in the west of England.

Bomb disposal teams have been examining a number of vehicles near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire and dozens of homes in the surrounding area have been evacuated.

Here is a summary of what we know so far.

RAF Fairford is located in the Cotswolds, about four miles (6.4km) south of the town of Fairford, which sits along the River Coln.

The base shares a long history with the American military, and has recently been used by US warplanes as a staging post for defensive strikes on Iran.

Gloucestershire Police said they received a call about "three suspicious vehicles" travelling towards RAF Fairford at 00:45 BST on Sunday.

Five men were later arrested by its officers near Whelford, a village around two miles (3.2km) south-east of the base.

A bomb disposal team was also deployed to the village to examine a number of vehicles, police said, around which a 400m (1,312ft) cordon is in place.

Aerial pictures showed a remote-controlled robot approaching two stationary white vans in a wooded area, though its use has not been confirmed by police.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) is leading the investigation into the incident.

The US military said it was "working closely" with its UK counterparts "to monitor this situation, minimise impacts and ensure the safety of US personnel, their families, and the local community".

There has been large emergency service presence in the area since the early hours of Sunday, which Gloucestershire Police Temporary Chief Constable Maggie Blyth said would remain over the next few days.

Blyth told a news conference on Sunday evening that the force would continue to assist CTP and liaise with other national partners.

She also said she would leave any declaration of a "terrorist incident" to CTP.

The five men were initially detained on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act.

They were then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.

The men, who remain in custody, have not been named. Police have not said where they are being held.

Asked whether police were seeking other individuals in connection with the incident, Blyth said she believed the matter was "contained".

US President Donald Trump said those arrested were "looking to do big damage", adding: "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them."

BBC Your Voice has since received an image purporting to show the moment five men were arrested.

It showed detained men in Whelford, about 350m (1,148ft) from runway access at Crash Gate 6A at RAF Fairford.

The BBC has been unable to verify the original source but BBC Verify has geolocated the image and confirmed it appeared to be authentic.

Gloucestershire Police said displaced residents have been told they will not be able to return to their homes on Sunday night.

Overnight accommodation would be found by Cotswold District Council for those affected who were unable to stay with family and friends, according to Deputy Chief Executive David Stanley.

Eighty-five households were evacuated following the incident and urged to shelter at a nearby leisure centre.

Several people have told the BBC they were woken by police in the early hours of Sunday and ordered to leave.

"We just had to throw our clothes on and come. We didn't know anything," one resident, who named herself only as Jo, said.

Another resident, Jason, said: "It all happened very quickly. We just packed our stuff up and came here."

Several people in the leisure centre are still wearing their pyjamas, according to a BBC reporter there.

A unnamed resident of Whelford told the PA news agency she called police after she saw three vans "blocking the road" and a "large group of hooded and 'balaclava'd' men".

The resident said she was driving home in the early hours of Sunday morning when she saw people in the road.

"They would have seen the bright headlights," she said. "They probably thought we were the police (and) panicked."

She added: "It would appear that by doing so I just derailed whatever they were planning."

Another resident described the moment he said he saw police apprehend the suspects.

Jeff told the BBC he heard "shouting outside his front door", although he could not be sure where it came from.

He said he then looked out of his window and saw "people being held by police outside".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the incident was "deeply concerning" and the government would "always take every step necessary" to protect people.

His defence secretary, Wes Streeting, declined to comment on a live operation but said he had been in contact with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth.

Asked at a fringe event at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool whether there was any Iranian involvement, he said it was "far too early to comment or speculate, and it would be irresponsible for me to do so".

RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

The base was occupied by USAF Strategic Air Command during the Cold War and later the first Gulf War in 1991.

B-52 bombers were also deployed by USAF from RAF Fairford on raids to Iraq in 2003.

It was most recently used on 1 March, following a decision by former UK prime minister Sir Keir Starmer to allow the US to use UK bases - including RAF Fairford - for "defensive" strikes on Iranian capabilities.

Conflict was sparked across the Middle East after the US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February.

Iran responded by launching attacks on Israel and US-allied states in the Gulf.

articles.title: Yellowstone rangers remove 20,100 pieces of trash from geothermal areas in 2026, including more than 5,000 rocks and sticks, 280 visitor hats and over $18 in coins
articles.summary: Cleaning up litter may be one of the less glamorous parts of working as a national park ranger, but at Yellowstone National Park, the job is particularly
articles.body: Cleaning up litter may be one of the less glamorous parts of working as a national park ranger, but at Yellowstone National Park, the job is particularly important because trash can pose a serious threat to the park’s geothermal features.With more than 4.5 million visitors each year, Yellowstone rangers regularly remove litter from some of the park’s most popular areas, including Old Faithful and Midway Geyser Basin. While food wrappers, tissues and water bottles are among the common items found, strong winds can also send visitors’ belongings into the park’s hydrothermal features.According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS), Yellowstone’s geology team has removed more than 20,100 pieces of trash from geothermal areas so far in 2026. They have also collected more than 5,000 rocks and sticks and, surprisingly, 280 visitor hats.“No matter the type of debris, it needs to be removed,” the USGS said, explaining that foreign material can damage or permanently alter hydrothermal features by clogging water supplies, blocking or diverting runoff channels, or introducing chemicals and sediment.Among the hundreds of hats recovered this year are a FIFA 2026 Men’s World Cup hat, a baseball cap labelled “COWBOY HAT” and a Roblox bucket hat from St. Kitts and Nevis.After the 2026 season ends, hats that can be reused will reportedly be washed and donated to local organisations.Yellowstone’s hot springs are not wishing wellsCoins are another recurring problem for Yellowstone’s geothermal areas.“Contrary to (apparently) popular belief, hot springs are not wishing wells!” the USGS warned.The agency explained that coins can clog hydrothermal vents and harm bacterial and algal formations, with resulting damage potentially taking months or even years to recover.As of September 2026, Yellowstone staff had collected more than $18 in coins. Some had been deliberately tossed into hot springs and geysers, while others were likely dropped accidentally between boardwalk planks.The collection has included not only US currency but also pesos, yen, euros and Canadian dollars.Camera lens caps, pacifiers and hotel key cards among items foundThe park’s geology team has also recovered a surprising assortment of everyday objects this year.Some of the most frequently found items include 54 camera lens caps, 47 hair ties, 42 pencils, 36 pairs of sunglasses, 20 hotel key cards and 17 baby pacifiers.Some discoveries were considerably stranger. Among the items listed by the USGS were AirPods, golf tees, an inhaler, six Invisalign retainers, 15 fake nails, floss picks and a lump of glittery slime believed to be a children's toy.Other children's toys have also ended up in the park, including miniature figures, bouncy balls, fidget spinners and rubber ducks.The USGS also highlighted some of the staff’s favourite discoveries, including seven Polaroid photographs. Several of the photographs reportedly depicted the very hydrothermal features where they were found.Yellowstone souvenir pennies and Pokemon cards were also among the more unusual items recovered.Why removing trash from geothermal areas mattersThe litter cleanup is not simply about keeping Yellowstone looking pristine. The park’s hydrothermal features are delicate, and introducing foreign objects can interfere with their natural processes.The USGS said Yellowstone’s Geology Program staff, who are trained in safely navigating hydrothermal areas, carry out much of the removal work. Alongside collecting trash and other debris, they monitor chemical and temperature conditions, assess hydrothermal incidents and educate visitors.Visitors are encouraged to “stash their trash” by keeping wrappers, paper and other lightweight items securely inside pockets or bags, or disposing of them in trash cans.And for those visiting Yellowstone’s windy geothermal areas, the USGS has one final piece of advice: “If you’re adventuring in a windy area, consider tightening or taking off your hat.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump says men arrested at UK air base used by US were looking to do 'big damage'
articles.summary: FAIRFORD, England, Sept 27 (Reuters) - British police arrested five men on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences on Sunday near an air base that has...
articles.body:
A police officer blocks a road near the RAF Fairford airbase, in Fairford

FAIRFORD, England, Sept 27 (Reuters) - British police arrested five men on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences on Sunday near an air base that has been used by the US to strike Iran, after a tip-off that three vans had been seen heading to the military airfield.

US President Donald Trump ‌said the suspects had been looking to do "big damage" and had been under investigation by British and US authorities.

British counterterrorism detectives leading the investigation said police had ‌received a call about three suspicious vehicles that appeared to be travelling towards RAF Fairford in the west of England in the early hours of Sunday.

Five men were arrested by armed officers and later held on suspicion of preparation ​of a terrorist act. Police, who said they believed the incident was now contained, have not yet publicly stated who they assessed was involved.

An Iranian-linked motive is considered the most likely, a source familiar with the investigation said, while a Russian sabotage operation or an Islamist plot were also being looked at.

POLICE WORKING TO UNDERSTAND CIRCUMSTANCES

"We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody," Counter Terrorism Policing Senior National Coordinator Vicki Evans said in a statement.

"As you would expect we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident."

Police said ‌a 400-metre cordon was in place around the base as the ⁠bomb disposal unit investigated the vans. Local residents in 85 homes in a nearby village were evacuated and armed officers were patrolling the site.

The British government, which has given authorisation to the US to use bombers based at Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in ⁠the Strait of Hormuz, said Prime Minister Andy Burnham was being updated on the incident.

Burnham thanked the police and armed forces, saying on X: "I know today's incident near RAF Fairford will be deeply concerning for local residents and for many people following developments across the country".

Britain said in July its armed forces were ready to protect the country from any attack after Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned it not to ​allow ​US bombers to fly from Fairford, saying any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target.

"The ​arrest in the UK was fantastic," Trump told reporters, saying it was "an ‌amazing job".

"We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great ... We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," Trump added.

On Sunday morning the base was blocked by armed police while large machinery also prevented access, and Reuters witnesses said security had been increased at other bases used by the US, with armoured vehicles and soldiers at the gates of RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall in eastern England.

A local farmer told the Daily Telegraph newspaper she had alerted police after seeing the vans and men acting suspiciously as she drove home from a party.

"I saw a group of Middle Eastern-looking young guys running off through ‌the trees. Some of them had masks or balaclavas on, and they all scattered ahead of us ​as we drove back past," she told the paper.

"Some of them ran into the fields, and some of them ​turned to run towards the air base ... I mean, you don't see masked men ​running around at half one in the morning in the countryside near a secure air base and not have concerns."

Local councillor Tristan Wilkinson told ‌Reuters there had been a recent security alert at Fairford and surveillance ​had been stepped up.

"So there was a specific threat ​about six weeks ago from the Iranians on this base. At the time, there was increased surveillance around the area," he said.

A spokesperson for the US Air Force declined to discuss specific force protection measures at the base.

"The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the ​safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors, and ‌their families," the spokesperson said.

British ministers have also previously briefed providers of critical infrastructure on the threat posed by Russia, with the government increasingly concerned about ​possible sabotage operations and cyberattacks.

Russia denies mounting hybrid attacks on Western nations.

(Reporting by Toby Shepheard, Andrew MacAskill, Gerhard Mey and David Ljunggren; writing by Kate Holton, ​Elizabeth Piper and Michael Holden; Editing by Alexandra Hudson, Elaine Hardcastle, Alexander Smith and Alex Richardson)

articles.title: Bass angler couldn't use LiveScope, so he followed whitetail deer to find the fish instead
articles.summary: Kaden Buchmann used deer sightings to gauge fishing pressure at Norfork Lake, going wire-to-wire without forward-facing sonar to win $71,317.
articles.body: What do you do when you can't use LiveScope to find the bass? You ask the deer, obviously. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS Kaden Buchmann went wire-to-wire to win the first Bassmaster Elite Qualifier of the season Friday at Norfork Lake in Arkansas, finishing the three-day tournament with 42 pounds, 7 ounces. But the fun part is how the 22-year-old found some of those fish. Forward-facing sonar was not allowed for the Norfork event, one of three Elite Qualifiers that will ultimately determine which 10 anglers earn invitations to the 2027 Bassmaster Elite Series. So Buchmann had to find another way to figure out where bass might be hiding — and, more importantly, where 130-plus other anglers hadn't already been. His solution was to ask the locals. Well, the four-legged locals. With so many boats working a relatively small reservoir, Buchmann started watching the shoreline for deer. If deer were hanging out close to the water, chances were pretty good another angler hadn't just come ripping through that pocket and scared them off. "If I saw 15 deer in a pocket, I'd say, 'I'm getting bit here,'" Buchmann told Bassmaster. And, somehow, it worked. Buchmann spotted more than 30 deer during the opening day of competition — including a 9-point buck — and used their presence as a clue for finding areas that hadn't seen as much fishing pressure. He weighed 16 pounds, 7 ounces that day to take the tournament lead. TREY MCKINNEY SAYS BASSMASTER VETERANS MADE HIM EARN THEIR RESPECT BEFORE HISTORIC AOY SEASON Then he did it again. On Day 2, Buchmann once again spent part of his morning looking for deer and said he caught two quality bass in a pocket where he had spotted them. "We can't use (forward-facing sonar) this week, so you just have to fish where you think they're gonna be," he told Bassmaster. Simple enough. But not easy. To be clear, Buchmann did a whole lot more than follow deer around Norfork Lake. Bassmaster credited his speed, mental toughness and ability to stay away from other competitors as major factors in the win. He covered enormous stretches of the lake, kept his trolling motor running high and targeted everything from docks to shaded shoreline with a topwater bait and skipping jig. On the final day alone, he said four of the fish he weighed came from places he had never previously fished. "I fished the whole lake," Buchmann said after the win. "I fished from about 3 miles from Missouri, all the way down to a pocket by the Norfork Dam." It all added up to a wire-to-wire victory. Buchmann opened with 16-7, added 14 pounds on Day 2 and survived a tougher final round with another 12 pounds. His 42-7 total beat runner-up Cody Stahl by 1 pound, 14 ounces and earned Buchmann $71,317 along with an invitation to compete in the 2027 Bassmaster Classic at Lake Hartwell. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER There are still two Elite Qualifiers remaining before the 10 Bassmaster Elite Series invitations are handed out, so Buchmann has plenty of work left to do. But now that his deer-scouting secret is out, don’t be surprised if there are a few more anglers watching the shoreline next time. Love all things fishing and outdoors? articles.body: The US military has rejected claims by Iran's Revolutionary Guard that it seized an advanced American underwater vehicle carrying out surveillance in the Strait of Hormuz.US Centcom spokesman captain Tim Hawkins told Al Jazeera that the US retains "positive control of all of our operational drone assets," dismissing the IRGC's claim as "clearly desperate."Earlier today, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had captured a second advanced US unmanned underwater vehicle, the Remus 600, in the Strait of Hormuz.The IRGC said the operation had been carried out through a "coordinated and complex operation" involving military intelligence and electronic warfare capabilities."With the help of God Almighty, the IRGC navy soldiers, through a coordinated and complex operation with intelligence and electronic warfare, were able to trap an advanced UAV of the American terrorist army that was operating in the Strait of Hormuz for the purpose of espionage," the statement read.Iranian officials alleged that the underwater drone had been conducting espionage missions within the strait. IRIB reported that the captured vehicle had been handed over to specialist military technicians for analysis and to recover its stored data.Previous captureEarlier this month, the IRGC captured a US uncrewed submarine near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.Iranian state media identified the vessel as a Dive-LD, a large autonomous underwater vehicle manufactured by California-based defence firm Anduril. According to the company, the 5.8-metre submersible is capable of carrying out missions such as mine countermeasures, seabed mapping, intelligence gathering and the inspection of underwater infrastructure including cables and pipelines."We trapped one of the most modern, intelligent and unmanned submarines of the terrorist American army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. This submersible is equipped with the latest technologies," Tehran's navy said in a statement carried by the state media.In response, a Pentagon spokesperson said the underwater drone had malfunctioned "more than a day ago.""It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations. It's only going to [be resolved] through diplomacy and negotiation," he said. "But I think if there's a deal to be made, President Trump is a businessman, he's a dealmaker, and I think he'll make the deal." articles.title: Sure, you may not need a towel warmer, but here’s a case for why one may be helpful to you
articles.summary: Make your post-shower experience feel more luxurious by heating your towel in a towel warmer — experts share what to look for when shopping.
articles.body: Picture this: You’ve just finished a hot, steamy shower. You turn off the water and step out into the cold air. Not so pleasant, right? But now imagine that you’re wrapped in a warm towel. That picture just became a whole lot more luxurious, didn’t it? A towel warmer can do more than just give you cozy vibes, says Michael Tidwell, CEO at Only Towel Warmers, an online towel warmer retailer. “A towel warmer can also serve several other purposes, such as warming the bathroom, drying towels for multiple uses and helping with mold and mildew caused by the wet fabric sitting around.” If you tend to really wet your towels after a shower, this could help you go through fewer towels in a week. Additionally, if you have a pet that you bathe at home, a warm towel can make the bath process a little less uncomfortable for them. And towel warming racks can be useful for drying bathing suits and other items. So while a towel warmer can feel like it only serves the purpose of luxury, it’s also practical. To help you shop for one, I spoke to Tidwell about what features to consider, then sourced highly-rated options in a range of prices. articles.title: Eviction of 87-year-old sparks encampment protest in Madrid over housing crisis
articles.summary: Protesters outraged by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman camped overnight in Madrid’s historic Puerta del Sol plaza, where more demonstrators — including multigenerational families — joined them on Sunday for a second day of protests over Spain’s housing crisis.
articles.body: MADRID — Protesters outraged by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman camped overnight in Madrid’s historic Puerta del Sol plaza, where more demonstrators — including multigenerational families — joined them on Sunday for a second day of protests over Spain’s housing crisis. Tens of thousands marched through Madrid on Saturday to protest the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal from the apartment in the upscale Retiro neighborhood where she had lived for more than seven decades. The demonstrators are demanding stronger tenant protections, measures to combat fraud and a ban on evictions when alternative housing is unavailable. Many refused to leave after Saturday’s march and pitched tents in Puerta del Sol for the night. “The housing situation is unsustainable,” said Natalia Navarro, a 27-year-old actress who was among those camping out at the plaza. “We are all out on the street because we are fed up.” “The wave of indignation and anger that has been unleashed is now unstoppable,” said Alicia del Río, a spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants’ Union, which led the protests. “We will remain here” until the government passes new laws, including indefinite rental contracts, and stops evictions like Abascal’s, del Río told journalists at the plaza on Sunday. Spain’s Socialist-led government is expected to announce new measures in its weekly cabinet meeting next Tuesday. Eviction ‘sparked this social unrest’ On Sept. 23, Abascal was carried from her apartment on a stretcher and placed in an ambulance as supporters — who had tried unsuccessfully to stop the eviction — chanted her nickname, “Maricarmen.” “I haven’t managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what’s theirs,” Abascal said in a video recorded from her hospital bed after the eviction. Images of the eviction spread widely across Spain, fueling outrage and criticism of public authorities and real estate investment companies accused of pricing residents out of their homes. Critics often refer to such companies as “vulture funds.” “Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest,” said Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher who took part in Saturday’s protests. Speaking at a Socialist Party rally in Madrid, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez addressed Abascal directly: “I have a message for you, Maricarmen: the government is working around the clock to bring a Royal Decree on housing next Tuesday. And I ask parliamentary groups to make one last effort to have it validated in the National Parliament for Maricarmen.” Abascal has criticized Sánchez and blamed him for her ordeal. “Does he not realize the quantity of evictions that there are daily?” she asked during an interview with Spain’s state broadcaster RTVE the day before she was forcibly removed from her home. “Does he not realize, or does he not want to realize?” A home for seven decades Spanish media reported that Abascal’s father first rented the apartment in 1956 and that she remained there as a tenant under rent controls after her parents died. The building changed ownership in 2018, and Abascal was offered the opportunity to buy the apartment but could not afford it, according to the Madrid Tenants’ Union. Urbagestión, an investment fund that later bought the unit, raised her monthly rent from 500 euros ($570) to 2,650 euros. It subsequently lowered the rent to 1,650 euros, which Abascal still could not afford on her pension, the union said. Rising costs and a growing housing shortage Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the market, despite strong economic growth in Europe’s fourth-largest economy. Incomes have not kept pace with the rising housing costs, and analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth in cities have placed further pressure on the limited housing supply. The Bank of Spain estimated that the country had a shortage of about 550,000 homes last year, with Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia accounting for a substantial share. The demonstrations in the symbolic Madrid plaza this weekend reminded many in Spain of the historic demonstrations starting May 15, 2011, when members of the “indignados movement” camped for 28 days straight, sparking similar sit-ins across the country and the world. That movement was a reaction to evictions and other issues following a global economic crisis, including unemployment, austerity measures and corruption. Estefania Molina, a political scientist and columnist, said the stakes of popular frustration are growing. In 2011, “people protested because they couldn’t buy an apartment.” “Today, the protest is about not being able to rent a room in someone else’s home,” she told Spanish television. Spain ranks near the bottom of countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development for subsidized public rental housing, which represents less than 2% of the country’s housing stock. The European Union average is 8%.

articles.title: Giant pandas arrive in Atlanta as part of 10-year US-China agreement
articles.summary: The two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, arrived from southwestern China.
articles.body:
Two giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, have arrived in the US state of Georgia on a 10-year loan as a soft-power gesture from China.

A new agreement between Zoo Atlanta and the China Wildlife Conservation Association makes Atlanta one of three zoos in the US to house giant pandas .

The diplomatic gifts departed early on Sunday from Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport in southwestern China, according to Chinese state media. They arrived after the high-level three-day Washington summit with China last week, where closed-door talks between United States President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping yielded no major policy breakthroughs on prickly issues such as AI, trade, Taiwan and the war with Iran.

Although the pandas’ transfer had been finalised back in April, Xi officially announced the arrival timeline on Thursday at the White House, noting that the black and white mammals could reach Zoo Atlanta from the Chengdu Research Base, China’s premier hub for giant panda conservation, breeding and research, within the next few days. The dispatch of the vulnerable species aimed to signal a renewed bilateral friendship between the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies.

Ahead of their arrival, Zoo Atlanta had upgraded its panda habitats and secured a stable, long-term supply of locally grown Atlanta bamboo, which shares a near-identical climate with Chengdu.

The bears completed a 16-hour charter flight across the International Date Line, landing in Atlanta, Georgia, shortly before 7:00am (11:00am GMT).

Midway through its journey through Alaska, the FedEx Boeing 777 had spiked to the top of Flightradar24’s global tracking charts.

Steamed corn buns, bamboo shoots and carrots were prepared to keep the pandas nourished during their flight, Chinese state-run media reported. The US also mobilised a specialised care team to accompany the duo on their flight, they said.

A spokesperson for the zoo told Al Jazeera that their team had “done everything possible to accommodate them”, but a definitive timeline for their arrival – much less their public debut – remains “unconfirmed”.

“This is a thrilling day for Zoo Atlanta and a historic moment for the City of Atlanta, the state of Georgia and beyond,” Zoo Atlanta President and CEO Raymond B. King said in a statement. “We are elated to welcome Ping Ping and Fu Shuang and could not be more excited about sharing that joy with our Members, guests, city and community in the coming weeks.”

Zoo visitors will have to wait a while to see Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, officials said. The bears will be quarantined for about a month in a biosecure area of the wildlife park’s new giant panda complex. The zoo last had pandas in 2024.

Ping Ping, a male, and Fu Shuang, a female, were born in 2020.

Globally revered, the iconic furry animals have been sent across the globe for decades, serving as diplomatic emissaries loaned by China under its infamous “panda diplomacy” initiative through soft-power projection. Beijing leverages the animals’ immense public appeal to cultivate international goodwill, seal lucrative trade deals and burnish its geopolitical image abroad. Similarly, when foreign relationships fray or tensions arise, Beijing lets the loan agreements expire.

Xi has said this latest loan programme was an example of “friendship between the Chinese and Americans”.

Last week’s summit was Xi’s first visit to Washington in more than a decade and the second meeting this year with Trump.

Tangible outcomes of the meetings remain modest , restricted to a two-month extension of the trade truce, Beijing’s revival of giant panda loans and Xi’s support for Trump’s rebranding of artificial intelligence as “super intelligence”.

articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: Why JD Vance's reshoring message is a perfect fit for struggling small towns like St. Cloud
articles.summary: St. Cloud, Minnesota's struggling downtown could be revitalized by JD Vance's reshoring agenda, but Somali immigration and fraud concerns loom large.
articles.body: Three weeks ago in Dallas, at the midterm convention, Republicans chose to put Vice President JD Vance in the spotlight, to lead the troops to November. His speech, about the future of the nation, could have been addressed directly to the town of St. Cloud, Minnesota, and its environs. In those remarks, referring to the future of his own kids, Vance said, "I want, whether they work in tech or manufacturing, American businesses to hire American workers, to rely on American people and to ensure that we build the next generation of great American products with American hands." You can almost hear those words echoing around the historic downtown of 19th century red brick, and it is a bit of a puzzle, because usually it is fairly obvious whether a city of this size — about 80,000 souls — is ascending or descending. But St. Cloud seems, well, stuck in the middle. THE ONE LINE FROM JD VANCE’S GOP KEYNOTE THAT REVEALS HIS VISION FOR AMERICA On the positive side of the civic ledger is the fact that the businesses that are open seem to be thriving. It's not in every minor metro downtown that you see packed restaurants for lunch on a Tuesday. There were also volunteers out painting the planters that line the sidewalk, another very positive sign of civic engagement. On the downside, almost half of the available commercial space is empty — like a handsome hockey player with some missing teeth — and foot traffic, at least for now, is not heavy enough to support many more retailers. Rob, now in his 40s, went to college at the nearby university in the early 2000s and told Fox News Digital, "Back then downtown was packed every night, you could barely move, I don’t think it's ever getting back to that." When I asked how he thought the town was doing, he said, "Better these days, better since COVID, but it's kind of plateaued," and he was not the only person I spoke to who used that particular word. One that can also be applied to much of the broader nation. Janice, another long-time resident dating back to the 1990s who works in real estate, set the date of the town’s downturn a bit earlier, with the closing of Herberger's department store — which opened in 1927 and shut down for good in 2018. "It’s a huge hole, right in the heart of downtown," she said, "and there isn’t anything to fill it." It was around this time that several factories in the area also closed down. To add insult to injury, in 2019, St. Cloud State University dropped its football program, never a great sign for a college town. But there are seeds of growth as well, and one of the planters, Chad O’Brien, opened a vintage store downtown in March 2025, just after Trump’s inauguration, and now has two on the same block, as businesses bubble up to life. "I think that the way the downtown works, the way that it draws people in, our business model and structure and the things that we sell seems like a really good fit," O’Brien told Fox News Digital, though he also said that more people living in the area would certainly help. Ultimately, this is why Vance’s mission to reshore manufacturing and reward firms that stay in America is such a perfect fit for St. Cloud. Honestly, a handful of businesses, with a few thousand jobs, could easily bring some of the hustle and bustle back. Perhaps one big plant with 1,500 factory jobs that can fill the single-family homes that semicircle the city, and a big tech firm hiring 300 to 500 younger workers to live downtown in walking distance to the bars and eateries. In a city this small, that's all it takes to make a difference. The biggest concerns you hear in St. Cloud surround the Somali immigrant community, but this issue is actually two distinct problems — both of which are firmly in the Vice President’s portfolio, the first being the massive fraud scandal. VICE PRESIDENT VANCE SAYS MIGRANT COMMUNITIES SHOW 'CLEAR PATTERN' IN FEDERAL FRAUD AS INVESTIGATIONS WIDEN Even on the ride back to the airport, Lynn, who also works in the beauty industry, told me of a ride she had given recently where an immigrant woman was bragging to her friend that she had just secured government-subsidized housing — but her boyfriend already had it, so they were going to rent hers out for cash. I could see Lynn’s knuckles whiten on the steering wheel as she said, "It just makes me so mad, I want to help the poor, but this can’t be the way." Everyone can agree that the fraud is bad, and hopefully, that the efforts spearheaded by Vance to stop it are good. But, the second part of the Somali issue is trickier and more intractable. It is the cultural component, another strong theme in Vance’s convention speech, and here opinions vary. Several people I spoke with expressed deep frustration at the seeming unwillingness of Somalis to assimilate, but not everyone. Trey, in his late 20s, is the sales manager at a local phone store who hired a Somali to help with customers of Somali descent. "He’s worried that their kids are becoming too Americanized and losing their roots," Trey said, adding, "I do see some of that, a lot of the teenagers don’t even speak their language now." Another gentleman in his 60s, who I met at a fairly high-end lounge told me, "There is no downside to these immigrants, it is all upside and the only reason to be against it is racism." I gently suggested that there are certainly people who think they have non-bigoted objections, but he doubled down, "It’s only racism." Downtown, though, is the place where the cultural and economic concerns meet, or, in this case, do not meet, because just as is true with the Haitian community in Springfield, Ohio, the Somalis in St. Cloud are not to be seen downtown — living instead, almost exclusively in their own enclave. The influx of Somali immigrants has not revitalized downtown because they don’t go there. A few thousand blue and white collared native-born workers absolutely would. More broadly, the Somali community sends so much of its income back to Somalia, money not being reinvested in St Cloud, that their overall economic contribution has to be questioned. Just northwest of St. Cloud is Sauk Centre, Minnesota, the real-life inspiration for Sinclair Lewis’ seminal novel Main Street, which over a century ago captured the uniqueness of the American small town — something that still charmed so many foreign World Cup travelers this past summer. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In these towns, like St. Cloud, and there are hundreds, Vance’s message is a perfect fit. His blend of America first and reshoring jobs to small communities truly does resonate, and makes sense. Just as Vance and his muscular populist message kicked off the midterms for the GOP, in October, it must carry it through. In other words, Mr. Vice President, are you ready for your close-up?

articles.title: Section of China's Great Wall damaged by two decades of illegal coal slag dumping
articles.summary: A remote stretch of China's Great Wall near Beijing has suffered lasting damage after being used for almost 20 years as a dumping ground for coal-mining
articles.body: A remote stretch of China's Great Wall near Beijing has suffered lasting damage after being used for almost 20 years as a dumping ground for coal-mining waste.According to a report by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, the wall's Guojiayao section, located in Shanxi province, first sustained damage in 2007 when an unlicensed mining operator, Ningwu Chaokai Coal Industry, cut a trench through the wall to discard excavation debris. In 2013, several mining teams merged to form Shenda Chaokai Coal Industry, which continued exploiting the breach to dump slag rather than transport it along longer mountain routes.CCTV reported that local authorities failed to act on repeated warnings from whistleblowers dating back to 2015, allowing the damage to continue unchecked for nearly two decades and eventually leaving a six-metre gap in the historic structure.Because of its isolated location, the lesser-known Guojiayao section was particularly exposed to neglect, even though China's 2006 Regulation on Protection of the Great Wall requires heritage authorities to take immediate action and alert higher-level officials whenever damage is reported. The law also mandates the placement of physical boundary markers, yet these were not installed along the Guojiayao stretch until 2025, CCTV said.Local officials reportedly told the broadcaster that the damage had gone unaddressed for years owing to poor conservation practices and infrequent inspections.As news agency PTI cited Hong Kong based SCMP, Provincial authorities only intervened this past March, when sustained public complaints and media coverage prompted Shanxi to set up a special task force to investigate the company's alleged illegal mining and heritage destruction.The firm was subsequently fined a total of one million yuan (US$149,000) for unauthorised construction within a protected cultural relics zone and for severe damage to the site, and its former executive and controlling figure were detained in May.CCTV noted that similar unmonitored mining has caused serious damage to other Great Wall sections in Ningwu.On Tuesday, the Ningwu county government pledged a sweeping crackdown on heritage damage and illegal slag dumping, promising emergency repairs, structural reinforcement, ecological restoration, and disciplinary action against officials found to have neglected their duties.You use AI every day. articles.body: Three people were killed and four others injured after an argument escalated into gunfire at an after-hours strip club in Michigan's Detroit early Sunday, police said. articles.title: Chettinad mansions, built two centuries ago, tell a story of local, sustainable architecture
articles.summary: Christ University study surveys 1,082 Chettinad mansions, highlighting sustainable features and crafts in a new digital repository with VR, Chettinad Heritage Explorer.
articles.body: Chennai: A study by researchers shows that the architectural marvel that is a Chettinad mansion has sustainable features such as rainwater harvesting, temperature regulation, locally made floor tiles and crafts such as woodwork.Researchers from Christ University in Bengaluru have surveyed more than 1,082 houses and mansions in 12 villages across Sivaganga and Pudukottai districts to create a digital repository, ‘Chettinad Heritage Explorer’, where visitors can see each building’s age, occupancy, preservation status, architectural style and heritage distribution. The oldest house in the region is about 200 years old.“Chettinad mansions were built with rainwater harvesting systems more than two centuries ago — rainwater from the courtyard of the building was taken to the oorani (tank) of the village through channels,” said Ajith Paul, researcher from Christ University.“Shaded verandahs and high ceilings facilitate natural lighting and cross ventilation. These courtyards were used as ceremonial spaces too. Chettinad architecture is still relevant as we can construct new buildings with its sustainable features,” said Anitha Suseelan, another researcher. The research team also included Biju K C from the university.Researchers analysed 11 parameters including heritage density, soil, groundwater, slope, geomorphology and land-use- and land-cover-related indicators. “Based on the analysis, we found the highest concentration of heritage buildings in areas which are environmentally suitable. Though it’s a dry region, the Nattukottai Chettiars or Nagarathars might have selected this area due to availability of water,” said Balakrishnan C, project coordinator and associate professor, department of computer science, Christ University.Researchers documented Chettinad’s living crafts such as Athangudi tiles, Kottan baskets, Kandangi handloom textiles, traditional jewellery, brass lamp casting, culinary practices, ritual foods, temple music traditions and everyday domestic rituals. They also recorded oral histories and folklore during their study. The homes are famous for using foreign materials such as Burma teak and Belgian mirrors.“The Chettinad houses are unique for wood carvings and courtyards. It’s very expensive to build such houses now. But we can use these ideas and crafts to revive the architecture,” said Visalakshi Ramaswamy, founder of M Rm Rm Cultural Foundation.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.title: More cameras, flood monitors for GCC’s command and control centre
articles.summary: GCC unveils ₹98.25 crore, 5-year ICCC upgrade plan: CCTV cameras 668 to 1,256, rain gauges 30 to 65, 40 floodometers, remote pump monitoring and GPS tracking.
articles.body: Chennai: Greater Chennai Corporation has drawn up a ₹98.25 crore, five-year plan to run and upgrade its Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC), expanding its network of flood-monitoring systems ahead of the northeast monsoon.The system will expand CCTV surveillance from 668 to 1,256 cameras and increase rain gauges from 30 to 65. GCC will get 40 new floodometers to measure and report waterlogging, along with an additional variable message display (VMD) to project public information. The plan includes internet-based remote monitoring of GCC’s 159 pumps, GPS tracking for 57 enforcement vehicles, 17 automated boom barriers and three regional ICCCs. No additional smart poles are proposed.The civic body has decided to retain CCTV footage for seven days instead of 30 days, and reduce ICCC manpower from 55 to 44. A GCC official said this was primarily a cost-saving measure. “Video storage is a major part of cloud spending,” the official said. The seven-day limit applies to video feeds, while application data, databases, system logs, backups, cybersecurity data and other system information will be retained.Of the ₹98.25 crore, ₹96.36 crore is recurring expenditure and ₹1.90 crore is one-time spending on project components and tech upgrades. Cloud services account for the largest share at ₹36.70 crore, followed by equipment upgrades and maintenance (₹34.13 crore), staff (₹16.60 crore) and internet connectivity (₹10.83 crore).The ICCC, functional since Dec 2020, is linked with 16 GCC departments. It pulls live data from cameras, rain gauges, flood sensors and GCC departments onto a single screen. Officials use it to track garbage collection, complaints and waterlogging, and to coordinate with Greater Chennai Police and disaster management teams. articles.body: Hamas had reportedly sent a warning to Israel before its October 7, 2023, attack, with the message conveyed through a Shin Bet channel.The warning came from Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, who cautioned that he would “shake the prisons”, said former defence minister Yoav Gallant on Sunday. articles.title: Nor’easter unearths fragments of 19th-century shipwreck on Nantucket
articles.summary: The powerful nor’easter pummeling the East Coast has uncovered what may be the remains of a 19th-century shipwreck on Nantucket’s shore Jason Graziadei, editor-in-chief of the Nantucket Current, spotted the wooden remnants on the Massachusetts island’s south shore Saturday and posted a video them.
articles.body: The powerful nor’easter pummeling the East Coast has uncovered what may be the remains of a 19th-century shipwreck on Nantucket’s shore Jason Graziadei, editor-in-chief of the Nantucket Current, spotted the wooden remnants on the Massachusetts island’s south shore Saturday and posted a video them. He believes they likely came from the Warren Sawyer, a wooden schooner that wrecked near Miacomet Beach 142 years ago. Fragments believed to be from the same ship first appeared in December 2022, when a Nantucket resident spotted them while biking along the island’s southern shore. Researchers examined archival, photographic, historical and archaeological evidence and concluded that the wreckage was “most likely” from the Warren Sawyer, according to a 2023 report from the Massachusetts Board of Underwater Archaeological Resources. The three-masted schooner wrecked there on Dec. 22, 1884, while traveling from New Orleans to Boston with 1,115 bales of cotton and 28 tons of scrap metal, the report said. More wreckage believed to be from the schooner appeared in February 2023, about a half-mile west of the first find, according to the report. “As far as I know, it’s the first time a piece of the wreck has resurfaced since 2022, early 2023,” Graziadei told NBC News on Sunday. “It’s certainly possible it could be from another wreck, but given the location and appearance, we said it is most likely the Warren Sawyer.” Jascin N. Leonardo Finger, deputy director of the Maria Mitchell Association, which runs a natural history museum on Nantucket, said in an email Sunday the newly exposed remnants may be from the Warren Sawyer, but “more investigation is necessary” to confirm their origin. The Massachusetts Board of Underwater Archaeological Resources did not respond to requests for comment on Sunday. The Egan Maritime Institute, which works to preserve Nantucket’s maritime history and assisted the board in previous efforts to identify Warren Sawyer wreckage, also did not respond to a request for comment. Shipwrecks near the island were not uncommon in the Warren Sawyer’s time, Leonardo Finger told The New York Times Saturday. Nantucket residents commonly scavenge item that wash ashore from wrecks, she said

articles.title: Tourism inks pact with SBI, ASI, kayaking body
articles.summary: Odisha Tourism signs MoUs with SBI, ASI and IKCA to boost homestays, heritage and adventure tourism, with new coaches and boats flagged off at Chilika.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: The tourism department on Sunday signed three MoUs with State Bank of India, Archaeological Survey of India and Indian Kayaking & Canoeing Association, seeking to boost homestays, heritage tourism and adventure tourism in the state.The agreements were signed as Odisha observed World Tourism Day 2026 with a focus on digital innovation, sustainable tourism, entrepreneurship and greater participation of local communities in tourism.Deputy chief minister Pravati Parida, who holds the tourism portfolio, said tourism should create livelihood and entrepreneurship opportunities for local communities, particularly youth, women, artisans and tourism service providers.She also stressed the need to leverage technology and emerging digital tools to improve destination discovery, access to tourism services and visitor experience.Chief secretary Anu Garg highlighted the need for coordinated efforts and institutional partnerships to strengthen the state’s tourism ecosystem while ensuring sustainable management of destinations and opportunities for local communities.Under the MoU with SBI, financial support will be extended to homestays, providing a fillip to community-led tourism and grassroots entrepreneurship. Provisional registration certificates under the Odisha Homestay Scheme were also distributed to 176 beneficiaries.Tourism department also signed an MoU with IKCA to promote adventure tourism in Odisha. Licences/registration certificates were distributed to adventure tour operators as part of efforts to formalise and expand adventure tourism activities.The agreement with ASI seeks to strengthen cooperation for heritage tourism. ASI director general Yadubir Singh Rawat, who addressed the gathering, highlighted the importance of preserving and promoting heritage assets as part of the tourism experience.OTDC luxury coaches were also flagged off during the programme to improve tourist mobility. articles.title: Snow brings down temperatures in HP’s upper reaches
articles.summary: Snowfall in Kinnaur and Spiti lowered temperatures in Himachal Pradesh, blocking 61 roads. Pilgrims stranded on the Kinnaur Kailash route were rescued.
articles.body: Shimla: Parts of Kinnaur and Spiti received snowfall on Sunday, bringing a sharp drop in temperatures across Himachal Pradesh’s upper reaches.Kinnaur’s higher areas, including Chitkul and Nako, received light snowfall, while lower areas witnessed rain. The snowfall began Saturday night and continued on Sunday.In the Spiti Valley, Kaza and Chicham recorded light snowfall. Rain also continued in lower Kinnaur for nearly 24 hours, with temperatures falling across the district.Rampur Bushahr, upper Shimla and Kullu’s Outer Seraj also received rain on Sunday.National Highway 305 was blocked near Tapri in Kinnaur due to mud flow, triggering a huge traffic jam. A car also got stuck in the mudflow.An official said restoration work had started. However, the road remained disrupted till the filing of this report.Traffic on the Reckong Peo-Kaza road was also disrupted at Maling Nala near Nako after continuous rockfall. Vehicles were halted as falling rocks made the stretch unsafe for movement.According to the State Emergency Operation Centre (SEOC), 61 roads remained blocked across the state on Sunday. Twenty-five roads remained shut for vehicular traffic in Lahaul-Spiti, followed by 19 in Mandi, six each in Kangra and Kullu, two in Sirmaur and one in Shimla district.In the Spiti sub-division, 24 roads were blocked due to the snowfall on Sunday.Pilgrims rescued (BOX)Over two dozen people, including 16 pilgrims, porters and guides, were rescued from the Kinnaur Kailash route after being stranded near Ganesh Park in Kinnaur due to heavy snowfall and icy winds. The weather suddenly deteriorated in the higher reaches, making further movement impossible.
